summary.text: A splitting field of a polynomial is an extension of minimal degree over the base field in which the polynomial splits.
Such splitting fields exist and are unique up to isomorphism.
The amount of freedom in that isomorphism is known as the Galois group of the polynomial, assuming it is separable.

facts.value: Splitting fields exist and are unique up to isomorphism

facts.label: For several polynomials
facts.value: The smallest field over which each one splits

facts.label: Normal extension
facts.value: A splitting field for a set of polynomials is called this

items.prompt: Two people build a splitting field step by step but pick different irreducible factors along the way. What happens to their final fields?

options.label: The final fields are isomorphic, even if the intermediate ones differ
The final fields are unrelated, so the choice matters a great deal
Only one of the two choices can produce a field
The final fields are equal, with identical intermediate steps

items.explain: Different choices of factors may give different sequences of subfields, but the resulting splitting fields are isomorphic.

items.prompt: An extension L is the splitting field of a set of polynomials over K. What special name does L get?

options.label: A prime extension
A normal extension
A trivial extension
A closed extension

items.explain: An extension that is a splitting field for a set of polynomials over K is called a normal extension of K.

items.prompt: Two splitting fields of the same polynomial are isomorphic, but there can be several ways to match them up. What does that amount of freedom measure?

options.label: The degree of the polynomial
The number of choices of irreducible factor
The size of the base field
The Galois group of the polynomial, when it is separable

items.explain: The amount of freedom in the isomorphism is known as the Galois group of the polynomial, assuming it is separable.

items.prompt: Many fields contain all the roots of a given polynomial. What makes one of them the splitting field?

options.label: It is the smallest field in which the polynomial splits
It is the largest field that contains the roots
It is the field with the fewest elements outside the roots
It is the field the polynomial's coefficients came from

items.explain: A splitting field is the smallest field over which the polynomial splits, generated over the base field by its roots.

items.prompt: In the step-by-step construction, how are two elements of the new field multiplied?

options.label: Multiply as polynomials and keep the remainder after dividing by f
Multiply their coefficients one place at a time
Add them as polynomials and then take the remainder
Multiply as polynomials and keep the full result

items.explain: Elements are polynomials of low degree; the product is the remainder of their ordinary product on division by f.

items.prompt: A polynomial already breaks fully into degree-one factors using numbers from the base field. What is its splitting field?

options.label: A bigger field with new roots added
The base field itself
A field with no elements besides zero
The complex numbers, always

items.explain: Nothing needs adding when the polynomial already splits into linear factors, so the base field itself is the splitting field.

paragraphs.heading: What a splitting field is
paragraphs.text: Take a polynomial whose coefficients come from some field. Its splitting field is the smallest extension of that field where the polynomial splits, meaning it breaks into linear factors. For example, x² − 2 cannot be factored over the rationals. Add √2 and −√2 to the rationals, and nothing more, and you get its splitting field.

paragraphs.heading: Existence and uniqueness
paragraphs.text: Splitting fields always exist, and any two splitting fields of the same polynomial are isomorphic. The freedom left in that isomorphism is the polynomial's Galois group, assuming the polynomial is separable. If the base field sits inside an algebraically closed field A, there is exactly one splitting field between them, generated by the polynomial's roots. For subfields of the complex numbers, existence is immediate.

paragraphs.heading: Related ideas
paragraphs.text: The splitting field of a whole set of polynomials is the smallest field over which every one of them splits. An extension that arises as the splitting field of such a set is called a normal extension. A Galois closure, built from a separable extension, is also a type of splitting field.

paragraphs.heading: How to build one
paragraphs.text: Start with the base field and factor the polynomial into irreducible pieces. Pick one irreducible factor f(X) and form the quotient ring of polynomials modulo f(X), which gives the next, larger field. The degree of this single step equals the degree of f(X). Repeat until the polynomial factors completely. The factor can be chosen freely at each step; different choices can give different chains of fields, but the splitting fields they end in are isomorphic.

paragraphs.heading: Building the complex numbers
paragraphs.text: Take the irreducible real polynomial x² + 1. In the quotient ring R[x] / (x² + 1), x² counts as −1, so every element reduces to the form a + bx with a and b real. Sending a + bx to a + bi is a bijective homomorphism, that is, an isomorphism, so R[x] / (x² + 1) ≅ C. Cauchy used this approach in 1847 to define the complex numbers.

paragraphs.heading: Finite fields
paragraphs.text: Over Fₚ, the splitting field of x^q − x is the unique finite field F_q, where q = pⁿ. Over F₇, the polynomial x² + 1 has no roots, so its splitting field is the larger field F₄₉. By contrast, x² − 1 already splits there as (x + 1)(x − 1), so its splitting field is F₇ itself.
